title: The $100 Lunches and Telethons That Paid for the Bionic Ear
dek: Refused research grants by sceptical reviewers, Graeme Clark funded his cochlear implant in the 1970s with service-club talks, telethons and collection tins.

story.company: Melbourne bionic ear programme (later Cochlear Ltd)
story.event: Raising money through luncheon talks, telethons and street collections after grant reviewers refused to fund the bionic ear
story.summary: Appointed the University of Melbourne's first professor of otolaryngology in 1970 with $6,000 for two years and no research grants, because reviewers thought a multi-channel cochlear implant would not work, Graeme Clark raised money from service-club talks, a $2,000 Apex Club gift and, from 1974 to 1976, three telethons underwritten by Sir Reginald Ansett, while his department shook collection tins in Melbourne. The money paid for a prototype that Clark implanted in Rod Saunders on 1 August 1978; government funding followed in 1979 and Cochlear Ltd was formed in 1982.
paragraphs: In 1970 Graeme Clark became the University of Melbourne's first professor of otolaryngology. He later recalled that the dean gave him $6,000 for two years and told him he would have to raise everything else himself; the department was not even finished. Clark wanted to build an implant that would let profoundly deaf people understand speech, an ambition he traced to childhood and to his deaf father, whom he had helped in the family pharmacy.

The usual route was shut. No money came from the National Health and Medical Research Council, he said, because the reviewers thought the device would not work, and he kept a whole file of unsuccessful applications. So he went after what he called soft money: $100 or $200 for speaking at a Lions or Rotary luncheon. He could see it would take a great many luncheons to pay for serious research.

The break came when the Apex Club of Melbourne gave him $2,000 and the gift made the ABC News. Sir Reginald Ansett, who was building up Channel 0 and wanted a telethon, saw the item, summoned Clark to his office and agreed to underwrite three telethons, which ran from 1974 to 1976. When the producers asked for a catchier name than cochlear implant, Clark offered one: the bionic ear. The telethons did not cover everything. Clark put up posters for gala concerts, and his department shook collection tins in the city centre; he ran a contest with his personal assistant over who could raise more, and won. There were many times, he said, when he could not fund some staff for more than a few months, a worry he mostly kept to himself.

The money let the team start the research and build a prototype. On 1 August 1978 Clark implanted it in Rod Saunders at the Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital, and the tests that followed showed a deaf person understanding running speech. Commonwealth funding followed in 1979, and Cochlear Ltd was formed in 1982 to make the device. Gus Nossal had warned Clark early on that he would spend half his time raising money. Clark has also said he never worked on Sundays.

quote.text: the gatekeeper said to him, 'Whom do you come from?' Tsze-lu said, 'From Mr. K'ung.' 'It is he,-- is it not?'-- said the other, 'who knows the impracticable nature of the times and yet will be doing in them.'
quote.thinker: Confucius (as described by the gatekeeper at Shih-man)
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: The gatekeeper may have meant it as a jibe, but it is an accurate portrait of one kind of persistence: seeing plainly that the times are against you and working anyway. Clark's reviewers judged his project impracticable, and he went on giving luncheon talks and shaking tins.

reflection: Raising money for work you believe in can feel like a distraction from the real work, even a small humiliation: the talks, the tins, the asking. Clark treated it as part of the job because nobody else was going to do it, and he was frank later about how much of his time it took and how much of the worry he carried alone.

He also said he never worked on Sundays, and that his wife and family came before the work. When money is thin and critics are confident, a day kept apart can look like something you cannot afford. Clark, with every reason to work all week, did not treat it that way.
invitation: Choose one evening or one day this week that you will keep entirely free of work, and tell someone at home which one it is, so that it is not only your decision to keep.

research_notes: The slate dated the telethon episode to 1978; the Encyclopedia of Australian Science dates the three telethons to 1974-1976, before the first implant in August 1978, so approx_date is 1974. Channel: Clark (2011) says Ansett was establishing Channel 0; the Encyclopedia of Australian Science and Science in Public say Channel 10. The story follows Clark's own wording. No source found gives the sums the telethons raised, so none is stated. The tin-shaking rival is Clark's 'PA' in the Academy interview and his 'secretary' in Aleteia; the story says personal assistant. Clark's own memoir (Sounds from Silence, 2000) was not available online to read in full, so the story rests on his 2011 oral history for the Australian Academy of Science, which covers the same years in his own words. The University of Melbourne's history pages and the NFSA's telethon article block automated requests and are not cited. Aleteia is a Catholic news site; it is used only for details that match Clark's own account. The Sunday remark comes from a National Portrait Gallery video interview and is presented as a general statement about his working life, not a claim about the 1970s specifically. The Analects passage is a gatekeeper's remark about Confucius, recorded in Book XIV; it is applied by analogy.
